Sixteen of the top 100 cities in China bear names that are false homonyms: different tones, same spelling.
Pingxiang in Gu angxi and Ji angxi are especially confusing (憑祥 / 凭祥 VS 萍鄉 / 萍乡).
Another such pair is Heshan in Guang xi and Guang dong (合山 VS 鶴山 / 鹤山).

Another such pair is Heshan in Guang xi and Guang dong (合山 VS 鶴山 / 鹤山).
Chinese people read characters and speak fluent Mandarin, so they are blissfully unaware that there might be a problem.
This is why foreign tourists should take special care when making travel arrangements.
Your originally intended destination might be off by hundreds of kilometers.

The problem of false homonyms in romanized Chinese was solved 73 years ago (1926), when GR Tonal Spelling was unveiled (AKA Gwoyeu Romatzyh 國語羅馬字or the National Phonetic Alphabet, version 2 國音字母第二式), a romanized companion to Bopomofo (1913, AKA Juhin Fuhaw 注音符號 or the National Phonetic Alphabet, version 1 國音字母第一式), devised to teach Chinese children to read.
The Chinese government promulgated GR Tonal Spelling in 1928.
Ever since then, it has appeared in dictionaries alongside Bopomofo, a tradition that has continued in Taiwan.

Both GR Tonal Spelling and Bopomofo (its older brother) are modified versions of the 1800-year-old tradition of fanqie (反切 fǎnqiè / faanchieh), where syllables are cut into I nitial Consonant, M edial Glide Vowel, R hyme and T one: IMRT.
In the fanqie system, syllables in different tones were spelled differently.
GR Tonal Spelling is based on a similar phonological analysis: systematic variations in spelling are used to mark tones (the rationale behind these variations is very frequently misunderstood).
GR is a mnemonic system that relies whenever possible on “green” spellings and dual-use semivowels. “Green” = use as few letters as possible, so vowels and tones are often combined into one letter.
The default (base, unmodified form) of all syllables that start with MNLR is the 2nd tone (mid rising); all other default spellings are used for the 1st tone (high level).
Because of their shapes, i-y-e are used as mnemonics to spell /i/ or the /j/ (similar to the “y” in y es /j ɛs/ or to y /tɔ j/) glide vowel in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd tone.
Similarly, u-w-o are used to spell the /w/ (as in w et /w ɛt/ or sho w /ʃo w/) glide vowel in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd tone.
When glide letters are unavailable or preempted for other roles, a mnemonic letter is added as a last resort: -r after the main vowel = 2nd tone; double vowel = 3rd tone; -h = 4th tone.
3rd tone: 撫州 / 抚州 F uu JOU (the first syllable is low and long [3rd tone], the second syllable is high level).
The leftmost column of each graphic in this post shows Bopomofo and GR Tonal Spelling, the two systems which are still in use in Taiwan.
Tone correspondences are indicated with dotted lines.
Note GR Tonal Spelling’s clever use of dual-use mnemonic letters.
The middle column shows the city name in traditional and simplified characters.
The rightmost column shows the city name in toneless Pinyin (the usual printed form), the provincial name and the fully-toned, correct Pinyin.
On the far right is a color-coded map showing the two provinces.

Unfortunately, the false homonym problem in foreign documents was un solved in 1958 when some smart people decided to create Hanyu Pinyin, a romanization that made it convenient for Chinese people to learn to read (the need for clear, unambiguous tone marking in documents for foreigners was not considered).
Most of GR Tonal Spelling’s vowel and consonant choices were adopted into Hanyu Pinyin without change (basic forms only).
Unfortunately, the tonal spelling principle was discarded in Mainland China.
In mainland China, the Sh a nxi (1st tone) VS Sh aa nxi (3rd tone) distinction is thus the only surviving relic of GR Tonal Spelling.

Because Hanyu Pinyin marks Mandarin’s four tones with tiny, hard-to-type, optional tone marks (omitted if inconvenient), foreigners have the false impression that Chinese only has ~400 different syllables (instead of 1200+ syllables if we include tones).
Toneless romanization helps to reinforce the stereotype that Chinese is unlearnable (so many homonyms!).
In turn, this encourages ignorant bigots to mock Chinese speaking Mandarin (ching, chang, chong is a common insult), a most unfortunate consequence.

The names reflect their geographical features, with "Shan" referring to mountains and "Xi" meaning west in Shanxi, and "Shaan" meaning "loose" or "sand" in Shaanxi.

Historical Significance: Both regions have rich histories that date back to ancient Chinese civilizations.
They were part of the same cultural and political developments over centuries, which contributed to the naming conventions.
Linguistic Roots: The names derive from different meanings but have similar phonetics, which can cause confusion.
Shaanxi is often associated with the area’s historical capital, Xi'an, while Shanxi is known for its mountainous terrain.

Colonial and Administrative Reasons: As administrative divisions evolved in China, particularly during the Qing Dynasty and the Republic of China, these names became standardized, leading to the retention of similar names despite their distinct identities.
Overall, while the provinces have similar names, they represent different regions with unique cultural, historical, and geographical characteristics.

Thus, when spelling 陕西 in the form of alphabet letters without its tone, it’s written as Shaanxi.

Why is one province of China called Shaanxi and another Shanxi?
Both provinces share the same “spelling” in Pinyin but are actually pronounced in different tones and written slightly differently in Chinese character.
The Chinese character for Shaanxi is 陕西, literally Shan West, and is pronounced as Shan3 Xi1.
Shan3 (陕) was the name of a region during Zhou Dynasty located in today’s Henan province.
The Chinese character for Shanxi is 山西, literally Mountain West, and is pronounced as Shan1 Xi1.
Shan1 (山) means mountain and in the case of Shanxi, it’s referring to Mount Xiao (崤山, pronounced as Xiao2 Shan1) in today’s Henan province.
